newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia budget, not Yeltsin op decisive for T-bills.
newsitem.headline: Russia budget, not Yeltsin op decisive for T-bills.

text.p: Yields on Russian government securities will edge down at most if President Boris Yeltsin fully recovers from his forthcoming heart operation but would soar if he dies, bond market analysts said on Monday.
Only a fatal outcome would have a serious impact on the market, sending prices plummeting, they said.
"All markets will panic, the most nervous operators will sell off, which will lead to a fall in prices and rise in yields," said Andrei Yashchenko, fixed-income analyst at United City Bank.
But whether Yeltsin survives or not, the main long-term influence on the market will be the government's ability to collect taxes and set a sustainable fiscal policy, the analysts said.
"Even if the Yeltsin factor goes, the budget issue still remains a serious problem," said Dmitry Falkovich, fixed-income trader and analyst at Alliance Menatep.
Doctors are meeting on Monday to decide whether Yeltsin is fit for a bypass heart surgery this week.

Konstantin Demchenko, head of the government securities department at Natsionalny Rezervny Bank, said the average yield on T-bills, now around 50 percent, would break resistance of 60 percent if the Russian president died.
Three-month paper would be the least affected, said Nicholas Jordan, head of capital markets at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, seen as a steady reformist, would take over for three months if Yeltsin dies or is incapacitated to prepare new elections.
UCB's Yashchenko argued that the impact on longer dates would be limited as primary dealers would stop yields rising too sharply.
UCB advised investors not to take the Yeltsin factor into account when making investment decisions, he said.
"Under the most unfavourable outcome, the succession is guaranteed," he said. "A representative of the current ruling group is most likely to win the repeat election."
A full recovery by Yeltsin will not of itself dispense with the serious economic issues faced by Russia, Jordan said.
Failure to collect taxes is the most difficult problem. State coffers received only 74 percent of budgeted revenues in the first nine months.
The International Monetary Fund last month delayed payment of the next tranche of its $10 billion loan to Russia because of worries about poor budget revenues.
One possibility is that Yeltsin survives the operation but turns out to be incapacitated, and new elections are necessary.
But the initial news of a successful operation in this case would push down yields, although budgetary problems would stop them falling below 45 percent, Yashchenko said.
"For the T-bill market political stability is the main thing and it will be present even if Yeltsin does not come back to power."
Current high yields are due to a combination of worries about Yeltsin's health and the budget problems, the analysts said.
Other factors influencing yields are the central bank's exchange rate policy, and the extent to which foreign investors can enter the market.
